facts.text: Composer Gordon Goodwin arranged this opening theme. He later wrote an Emmy-nominated big-band piece inspired by the film's music for his Big Phat Band.
Writer Costa Dillon got the idea as a San Diego teen after seeing the Japanese film Matango, shown on US TV as Attack of the Mushroom People. He thought: how dumb is this? Then made it sillier.
The giant tomatoes were foam. After PVC and papier-mache failed, the crew built them from soundproofing material from BART train cars, per Mental Floss.
TMDB lists the budget at $100,420 and the worldwide gross at $567,000, a decent return for a parody made by college buddies with money from friends and family.
This conference room scene was parodied in the opening titles of the 2022 anime series Chainsaw Man, 44 years after the film came out.
Japanese scientist Dr. Fuji Nokitofa knocks a picture of the USS Arizona into a goldfish tank. The Arizona was sunk by Japan at Pearl Harbor.
Dana Ashbrook, later Bobby Briggs in Twin Peaks, made his film debut here as an uncredited boy on a boat, at about age 10 or 11.
It began as a short made for a film class at UC Davis by Costa Dillon, John De Bello and Steve Peace. It was shot on Super 8 and earned an A. No known copies survive.
This press conference was shot in a high school auditorium. The production was non-union and ran on a shoestring.
Before the film, De Bello and Steve Peace ran Four Square Productions in San Diego, taping high school and junior college football games. Dillon joined later.
Variety was not kind on release, writing that the film "isn't even worthy of sarcasm." It has since become a cult favorite.
Relatives of the filmmakers helped finance the movie, and family members pop up in small parts. Most of the cast had never acted before, and several never acted again.
"Puberty Love" is sung by Matt Cameron, then about 14 with a changing voice. He was director John De Bello's neighbor and later drummed for Soundgarden and Pearl Jam.
Co-writer and producer Steve Peace plays Wilbur Finletter and did his own stunts. For the street-drag scene, a wheeled board was put under his stomach. He was also knocked out in one rehearsal.
A fourth Four Square member, Michael Grant, was a college roommate of John De Bello, Costa Dillon and Steve Peace and worked on the 1976 short, but skipped the feature for school.
Co-writer Steve Peace later became a California legislator: Assembly from 1982 to 1993, then State Senate until 2002.
The film was shot on 35mm Kodak 5247 negative, unusual for a micro-budget movie. That polished look is one reason people assumed it cost more than it did.
Costa Dillon says the crew used two kinds of tomatoes: cheap rotting "stock tomatoes" to smash and throw, and photogenic "star tomatoes" saved for close-ups.
Many scenes were shot on the UC San Diego campus. In 2007, director John De Bello admitted the crew borrowed lab coats from empty campus offices.
Rotten Tomatoes puts the film at 27% on 11 reviews. Metacritic scores it 9 out of 100, a fittingly rotten result for a movie about tomatoes.
This is the only entry in the franchise that never features or mentions Dr. Gangrene, the mad scientist who shows up in the sequels.
In 1983, producer Steve Peace, by then a California assemblyman, sponsored a bill requiring tomatoes be labeled "vine picked" or "artificially ripened." The AP joked he owed a debt to the tomato.
In March 1980, one theater billed the film as a double feature with Return of the Pink Panther, a very odd pairing.
Rue Morgue's Michael Gingold wrote in 2018 that it may be "one of history's most misunderstood films": an attempt at intentional comedy, not an accidental so-bad-it's-good movie.
Most of the army uniforms came from Goodwill thrift stores.
When John Astin, who played Professor Gangreen in the sequels, asked director John De Bello if he should watch the original, De Bello said: "Don't bother."
Director John De Bello on the bad reviews: he was "greatly honored" that someone had to make the worst vegetable movie, and asked why it couldn't be him.
The 1988 sequel Return of the Killer Tomatoes! is notable for an early role for a young George Clooney.
The film is name-checked in Trancers, Gremlins 2: The New Batch, Mars Attacks! and Eight Legged Freaks, among many others.
Author Kim Harrison admitted this film inspired her urban fantasy series The Hollows, set in a world where genetically engineered tomatoes killed much of humanity.
On January 13, 1990, the crew of space shuttle Columbia was woken with this film's theme song, a joke since Columbia was retrieving 12.5 million tomato seeds launched in 1984.
A remake was announced in 2008 by Kent Nichols and Douglas Sarine, creators of Ask a Ninja. By 2011 director John De Bello said they were no longer involved.
The stadium finale was shot in a single day at San Diego Stadium, and the extras wore their own outfits.
Among the crowd of "every screwball in San Diego County" was Ted Giannoulas, the San Diego Chicken.
The giant tomato's earmuffs were two bright green toilet seat covers.
